:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: Find the slope of the tangent to the curve $y = x^2 + \dfrac {1}{x}$ at the point where $x=2.$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Let $f(x)=x^2+\dfrac 1 x.$ The slope of the tangent at $x=2$ is equal to $f'(2).$ Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}+\frac{1}{x}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}+{x}^{-1}) \\  & =2\cdot x-{x}^{-2} \\  & =2x-{x}^{-2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we evaluate at $x=2$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(2) & =2(2)-(2{)}^{-2} \\  & =4-\frac{1}{4} \\  & =\frac{15}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent to the curve is $\dfrac{15}{4}.$

Find the slope of the tangent to the curve $y={x}^{7}-6{x}^{5}-2670x$ at the point where $x=3.$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
Let $f(x)={x}^{7}-6{x}^{5}-2670x.$ The slope of the tangent at $x=3$ is equal to ${f}^{′}(3).$ Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{7}-6{x}^{5}-2670x) \\  & =7{x}^{6}-30{x}^{4}-2670.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we evaluate at $x=3$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(3) & =7(3{)}^{6}-30(3{)}^{4}-2670 \\  & =5103-2430-2670 \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent to the curve is $3.$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: Find the slope of the tangent to the curve $y=3{x}^{4}-6{x}^{3}+\frac{1}{x}$ at the point where $x=2.$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
Let $f(x)=3{x}^{4}-6{x}^{3}+\frac{1}{x}.$ The slope of the tangent at $x=2$ is equal to ${f}^{′}(2).$ Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3{x}^{4}-6{x}^{3}+\frac{1}{x}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3{x}^{4}-6{x}^{3}+{x}^{-1}) \\  & =4\cdot 3{x}^{3}-3\cdot 6{x}^{2}-{x}^{-2} \\  & =12{x}^{3}-18{x}^{2}-{x}^{-2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we evaluate at $x=2$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(2) & =12(2{)}^{3}-18(2{)}^{2}-(2{)}^{-2} \\  & =96-72-\frac{1}{4} \\  & =\frac{95}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent to the curve is $\frac{95}{4}.$

Let $f(x)=({x}^{2}-1{)}^{3}+3.$ The slope of the tangent at $x=-1$ is equal to ${f}^{′}(-1).$ Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{d}{dx}\,({x}^{6}-4{x}^{4}+8{x}^{2}-4) \\  & =6{x}^{5}-4(4{x}^{3})+8(2x)-0 \\  & =6{x}^{5}-16{x}^{3}+16x.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we evaluate at $x=-1$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(-1) & =6(-1{)}^{5}-16(-1{)}^{3}+16(-1) \\  & =-6+16-16 \\  & =-6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope $m$ of the tangent to the curve at $x=-1$ is

$$
m={f}^{′}(-1)=-6.
$$

Let $f(x)=-2{x}^{2}+\frac{1}{(x-2{)}^{2}}.$ The slope of the tangent at $x=3$ is equal to ${f}^{′}(3).$ Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-2{x}^{2}+\frac{1}{(x-2{)}^{2}}) \\  & =-4x+(-2(x-2{)}^{-3}) \\  & =-4x-\frac{2}{(x-2{)}^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we evaluate at $x=3$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(3) & =-4(3)-\frac{2}{(3-2{)}^{3}} \\  & =-12-2 \\  & =-14.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $f(x)=2{x}^{4}-7{x}^{3}-6{x}^{2}-\frac{1}{x}.$ The slope of the tangent at $x=3$ is equal to ${f}^{′}(3).$ Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{4}-7{x}^{3}-6{x}^{2}-\frac{1}{x}) \\  & =2\cdot 4{x}^{3}-7\cdot 3{x}^{2}-6\cdot 2x+{x}^{-2} \\  & =8{x}^{3}-21{x}^{2}-12x+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we evaluate at $x=3$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(3) & =8({3}^{3})-21({3}^{2})-12(3)+\frac{1}{{3}^{2}} \\  & =216-189-36+\frac{1}{9} \\  & =-9+\frac{1}{9} \\  & =-\frac{80}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope $m$ of the tangent to the curve at $x=3$ is

$$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: Find the $x$-coordinate of the point on the curve $y=3x^2+1$ where the tangent line has a slope of $-1.$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Let $f(x)=3x^2+1.$ The slope of the tangent at the point $x$ is equal to $f'(x).$ Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3{x}^{2}+1) \\  & =3\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(1) \\  & =3\cdot 2x+0 \\  & =6x+0 \\  & =6x.\end{aligned}
$$

We now set $f'(x) = -1$ and solve for $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =-1 \\ 6x & =-1 \\ x & =-\frac{1}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent is equal to $-1$ at the point where $x=-\dfrac 1 6.$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: What is the slope of the tangent to the curve $y = x^4 + 3\sqrt [3]{x^2}$ at the point $(1,4)?$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
This time, we'll use $\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x}$ notation. First, we compute the derivative, which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{4}+3\sqrt[3]{{x}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{4}+3{x}^{2/3}) \\  & =4\cdot {x}^{3}+3\cdot \frac{2}{3}\cdot {x}^{-1/3} \\  & =4{x}^{3}+2{x}^{-1/3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at $x=1$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=1} & =4(1{)}^{3}+2(1{)}^{-1/3} \\  & =4+2 \\  & =6\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent to the curve is $6.$

Remember that the derivative of a function $f(x)$ represents the slope of the tangent line to the curve $y=f(x).$

For example, consider the curve $y=x^2$, shown below. If we want to compute the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $A(1,1),$ then we compute $f'(x)$ and evaluate $f'(1).$

![](images/63/63f675532755376a733f2f0cad2b40e55f19b3278c1bcc5e8cb355fc6bdac277.png)

If $f(x)=x^2,$ then $f'(x) = 2 x$ by the power rule. Substituting $x=1$ into $f'(x)$ gives
$$
f'(1) = 2 (1) = 2.
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent to the curve $y=x^2$ at the point $A$ is $2.$

:topic/knowledge-points.:knowledge-point/title: Differentiating a Power Function Using the Constant Multiple Rule

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: If $y=-\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{x}}$, find $\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x}$.
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
We first rewrite the function as

$$
y = -\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{x}} = -\dfrac{3}{x^{1/2}} = -3x^{-1/2}
$$

Then, we apply the constant multiple and power rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{dy}{dx} &= \frac{d}{dx}(-3x^{-1/2}) \\
&=-3 \cdot \frac{d}{dx}(x^{-1/2}) \\
&=-3 \cdot \left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)x^{-3/2} \\
&= \frac{3}{2}x^{-3/2} \\
&= \frac{3}{2\sqrt{x^{3}}}
\end{aligned}
$$

:topic/knowledge-points.:knowledge-point/title: Differentiating a Negative Power Function Using the Constant Multiple Rule

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
The function $f(x)$ is the sum of three power functions. So, we apply the sum rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
f^{′}(x) &= \frac{d}{dx}(x^{4} - \frac{1}{x^{2}} + x) \\
&= \frac{d}{dx}(x^{4} - x^{-2} + x) \\
&= \frac{d}{dx}(x^{4}) - \frac{d}{dx}(x^{-2}) + \frac{d}{dx}(x) \\
&= 4x^{3} - (-2)x^{-3} + 1 \\
&= 4x^{3} + 2x^{-3} + 1 \\
&= 4x^{3} + \frac{2}{x^{3}} + 1
\end{aligned}
$$

:topic/knowledge-points.:knowledge-point/title: Differentiating a Sum of Functions Without Constant Factors Using the Sum Rule

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Here, we convert the radical into a rational exponent, and we apply the addition, constant multiple, and power rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{dy}{dx} &= \frac{d}{dx}(2x^{3} + 6x^{1/2}) \\
&= \frac{d}{dx}(2x^{3}) + \frac{d}{dx}(6x^{1/2}) \\
&= 2 \cdot \frac{d}{dx}(x^{3}) + 6 \cdot \frac{d}{dx}(x^{1/2}) \\
&= 2 \cdot 3x^{(3 - 1)} + 6 \cdot \frac{1}{2} \cdot x^{(1/2 - 1)} \\
&= 6x^{2} + 3 \cdot x^{-1/2} \\
&= 6x^{2} + \frac{3}{\sqrt{x}}
\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Find the slope of each of the lines below.

![](images/e9/e901704deb02efe957129512148c97e42b45b4fdd1d0e3af451562cca2ed1181.png)
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
The slope of the vertical line is undefined. We can see this by choosing two points on the line, such as $(4,0)$ and $(4,1),$ and computing the slope between them:

$$
\begin{aligned}m=\frac{{y}_{2}-{y}_{1}}{{x}_{2}-{x}_{1}}=\frac{1-0}{4-4}=\frac{1}{0}=\text{undefined}\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand, the slope of the horizontal line is zero. We can see this by choosing two points on the line, such as $(0,3)$ and $(1,3),$ and computing the slope between them:

$$
\begin{aligned}m=\frac{{y}_{2}-{y}_{1}}{{x}_{2}-{x}_{1}}=\frac{3-3}{1-0}=\frac{0}{1}=0\end{aligned}
$$

:topic/knowledge-points.:knowledge-point/title: Slopes of Horizontal and Vertical Lines

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Calculate the slope of the line shown below.

![](images/48/48114216e210a4e4dfc353871bbfd16bd2beb480f5831c62189db9299e09f517.png)
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Note that the line passes through the points $(-2,0)$ and $(0,2).$ So, we let $(x_1,y_1) = (-2,0)$ and $(x_2,y_2) = (0,2),$ and compute the slope using the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}m & =\frac{{y}_{2}-{y}_{1}}{{x}_{2}-{x}_{1}} \\  & =\frac{2-0}{0-(-2)} \\  & =\frac{2}{2} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the line is $m=1.$

:topic/knowledge-points.:knowledge-point/title: Calculating the Slope of a Graphed Line

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: Calculate the slope of the line that passes through the points $(1, 5)$ and $(4, 2).$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
We let $(x_1,y_1) = (1,5)$ and $(x_2,y_2) = (4,2),$ and compute the slope using the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}
		m &= \dfrac {y_2 - y_1} {x_2 - x_1} \\
		    &= \dfrac {2 - 5} {4 - 1} \\
		    &= \dfrac {-3}{3} \\
		    &= -1
	\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the slope is $m=-1.$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Given the following graph, what can we say about the sign of the slope?

![](images/ff/ffa6dd91f72bc66c943e88aa764a64811391a00af162b40320ce3d90f96b16a4.png)
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Remember that slope is the amount the line rises vertically per unit that it runs horizontally.

Since the graph decreases ($\searrow$) as we go from left to right, the line rises by a negative amount.

Therefore, the slope of the line is negative.
